4: Basic Compiler techniques for exploiting ILP
Reducing the branch penalty with advanced branch predictions
overcoming data hazards with dynamic scheduling

questions.q: An enhancement speeds up 80% of a program's execution time by a factor of 10. What is the overall speed-up? (Two decimal places.)
In Flynn's classification, a processor that applies the same instruction to many data elements at once (as a GPU does) is:
questions.model: Single instruction, multiple data.

questions.q: A program executes 2 x 10^9 instructions with an average CPI of 1.5 on a 3 GHz processor. What is its CPU time in seconds?
questions.model: CPU time = IC x CPI / clock rate = 2e9 x 1.5 / 3e9 = 1.0 s.

questions.q: Why are standard benchmark suites such as SPEC used to compare processors, and why are their results summarised with the geometric mean of speed ratios?
questions.model: Suites of real programs give a representative, reproducible workload that vendors cannot tune for a single kernel. The geometric mean of ratios to a reference machine gives the same ranking whichever machine is the reference.

questions.q: A 32 KB, 4-way set-associative cache has 64-byte blocks. How many bits of the address are used as the set index?
questions.model: Sets = 32768 / (64 x 4) = 128 = 2^7, so 7 index bits.

questions.q: L1 hit time is 1 ns with a 5% miss rate; L2 hit time is 10 ns with a 20% local miss rate; main memory takes 100 ns. What is the average memory access time in ns?
Explain how a snooping write-invalidate protocol (such as MSI) keeps caches coherent when two processors read and then one writes the same block.
questions.model: Both caches hold the block in Shared state after reading. The writer broadcasts an invalidate on the bus; the other copy becomes Invalid and the writer's copy Modified. A later read by the other processor misses, the owner supplies or writes back the data, and both return to Shared.

questions.q: What does the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) cache?
questions.model: The TLB is a cache of page table entries.

questions.q: True or False: A virtual machine monitor (hypervisor) lets several operating systems share one physical machine while keeping them isolated from one another.
questions.model: True; the VMM virtualises the hardware for each guest and isolates them.

questions.q: A linear pipeline has 4 stages of equal delay. What is its speed-up over a non-pipelined unit when processing 100 tasks? (Two decimal places.)
questions.model: S = n k / (k + n - 1) = 100 x 4 / 103 = 3.88 (approaching k = 4 for large n).

questions.q: Explain how Tomasulo's algorithm uses reservation stations and register renaming to allow out-of-order execution.
questions.model: Instructions are issued to reservation stations that hold operands or tags of the producing units; renaming to station tags removes WAR and WAW hazards. Instructions execute when operands are ready, and results are broadcast on the common data bus to waiting stations and registers.

questions.q: A loop branch is taken 9 times and then not taken once, and the loop runs repeatedly. Compare the mispredictions per loop execution of a 1-bit predictor and a 2-bit saturating-counter predictor, in steady state.
questions.model: 1-bit: mispredicts at the exit (predicts taken) and again at the first iteration of the next run (predicts not taken): 2 per run. 2-bit: one not-taken outcome only weakens the prediction, so it mispredicts only at the exit: 1 per run.

questions.q: Read the assertion and reason about pipeline hazards and choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A structural hazard occurs when two instructions need the same hardware resource in the same clock cycle.
questions.reason: Separate instruction and data memories can remove some structural hazards.
questions.model: Both statements are true, but R describes a remedy rather than explaining what a structural hazard is.

questions.t: Basic Compiler techniques for exploiting ILP
questions.q: Explain how loop unrolling combined with instruction scheduling increases instruction-level parallelism, and state two costs of unrolling.
questions.model: Unrolling replicates the loop body, removing branch and counter overhead and exposing independent instructions that the compiler can reorder to hide latencies (using different registers). Costs: larger code (instruction-cache pressure) and more registers needed; leftover iterations need extra code.

questions.t: Reducing the branch penalty with advanced branch predictions
questions.q: What does a branch target buffer (BTB) store?
opts: The outcome of every past branch in the program
The predicted target addresses of recently executed branch instructions
The return addresses of procedure calls only
The contents of the instruction cache
questions.model: A BTB maps branch instruction addresses to predicted targets so fetch can continue without waiting for decode.

questions.t: overcoming data hazards with dynamic scheduling
questions.q: Register renaming removes the name-dependence hazards ___ and ___, but it cannot remove true data dependences (RAW).
questions.model: WAR (anti-dependence) and WAW (output dependence).

questions.q: Evaluate superscalar and VLIW multiple-issue designs for each product in the case and recommend one for each, with justification.
questions.case: A company designs two processors: (1) a low-power digital signal processor for audio equipment that runs a few fixed, highly regular filtering kernels compiled once, and (2) a laptop processor that must run unmodified commercial software from many vendors at good performance.
questions.model: (1) VLIW: the compiler schedules regular loops statically, so hardware is simpler and lower power; binary compatibility is not needed. (2) Superscalar with dynamic scheduling: hardware finds parallelism at run time in arbitrary code and keeps compatibility with existing binaries, at the cost of power and complexity.

questions.q: Compare message-passing and shared-memory multiprocessors in terms of programming model, communication cost and scalability.
questions.model: Shared memory: one address space, communication by loads and stores, easier programming but needs coherence and synchronisation; scaling is limited by the interconnect. Message passing: private memories, explicit send/receive, harder to program but scales to thousands of nodes because no global coherence is required.

questions.q: Design a multithreaded approach to multiply two 4096 x 4096 matrices on a 16-core centralized shared-memory machine. Describe the data partitioning, synchronisation, cache-friendly loop order and the factors that limit the speed-up.
questions.model: Partition result rows (or blocks) among 16 threads, so no two threads write the same element and no locks are needed; join at the end. Use blocked (tiled) multiplication with i-k-j order for spatial locality and reuse in cache. Limits: memory bandwidth, false sharing on boundary cache lines, load imbalance and thread start-up overhead (Amdahl's serial part).

questions.q: What are vector registers and vector chaining, and why do vector architectures suit scientific loops?
questions.model: Vector registers hold many elements and one instruction operates on all of them; chaining forwards results of one vector unit element by element into the next. Scientific loops apply the same operation to long arrays, so few instructions do much work with deep pipelining.
